100-the-story-of-a-patriot:
100%: The Story of a Patriot, by Upton Sinclair, was published by the author at Pasadena in 1920. Sinclair dedicates the book to his wife. She created, he says, its most charming character, Mrs Godd. The dedication insists, with comic care, that this Godd is Grecian and not Hebrew, so no one will charge sacrilege. The hero, Peter Gudge, is introduced through a meditation on accident.

Section 1 asks how a life hangs on a street corner turned right instead of left, a girl met, a marriage made. Peter's own turning comes as a bomb and a red scare sweep him from nobody to paid informer among radicals. Sinclair, the muckraking novelist of The Jungle, writes the postwar hunt for Reds from inside the informer's small, frightened mind. Patriotism at one hundred percent, the title promises, will be measured by what it buys and whom it betrays.
21125-the-boy-patriot:
Edward Sylvester Ellis, a hugely popular writer of boys' books, set this story in an earlier time. It appeared fifty years after its setting, published in 1863 by the American Tract Society. Blair Robertson of Fairport, on the coast of Maine, is its boy hero. The publishers hoped his example would prompt young Americans to serve God and country.

Rocky Maine shores, salt waves, and foam open a tale of a boy's faith and courage in wartime days. The short book mixes adventure with plain moral teaching, as Tract Society stories did. Ellis frames Blair's deeds as lessons for readers of his own Civil War generation, though the scene lies decades earlier.
21208-among-the-sioux-a-story-of-the-twi:
The Reverend R. J. Creswell spent forty years in missionary work, first among freedmen of the old Southwest and then among pioneers of the Northwest. His 1906 Minneapolis volume gathers sketches he had printed in periodicals. Its platform asks American education, homes, and rights for Indians, ending in citizenship.

Creswell knew many Sioux people personally and visited their homes, and missionaries told him their stories of hardship directly. The sketches cover the Twin Cities and the two Dakotas of his subtitle. An introduction by David R. Breed praises his long study of mission work among the Sioux. The book argues its cause through lives rather than statistics.
21292-brave-and-true-short-stories-for-c:
George Manville Fenn's name leads this children's collection, though he seems to have written only one of its stories, and not the title tale. Twelve items in all appear: nine short stories and three slight poems. Every story carries the theme of its title, brave and true, for readers of about seven or eight.

Settings jump from small boarding schools in the Home Counties to the Rocky Mountains. Several stories run unsigned, leaving their authors a small mystery. The book shows the lives of younger boarding school boys and girls of the nineteenth century, roughly eight to thirteen years old. Short, plain, and moral, it aimed well below Fenn's usual teenage audience.
21844-the-tale-of-turkey-proudfoot:
Turkey Proudfoot struts across Farmer Green's yard in this 1921 children's tale by Arthur Scott Bailey, part of his Slumber-Town Tales. Every hen turkey thinks him a wonderful creature with the most beautiful tail on the farm. When he spreads it and struts, they nudge each other and say so. The geese, less impressed, hiss at him from the frontispiece.

Chapters follow his pride through scrapes with geese, crows, and a strange gobble in the woods. Mrs. Wren gives advice, and cranberry sauce casts its long shadow near the end. Bailey teaches farmyard nature through comedy, as in his Jasper Jay. Proudfoot's vanity is his flaw and his charm. Small readers learn the turkey while laughing at his airs.
21884-the-faithless-parrot:
Tittums the cat and Fido the dog live happily in a fine house in Charles H. Bennett's picture tale, The Faithless Parrot. Fido falls in love with Tittums and confesses it by the hearth, paws on the fender, while she keeps her cool. Her sly sideways look tells him more than words. Then a gentleman from the tropics comes calling, a parrot with all the impudence of his race.

The parrot presses Tittums's paw to his heart and makes himself quite at home. Bennett designed and narrated the little book himself, and his drawings carry the joke. It is a Victorian comic tale for children about flattery and true hearts. The making-up scene, pictured at the front, promises the right end for Fido.
22462-slingshot:
Irving W. Lande wrote Slingshot, a science fiction story set under a great dome. Its man Coulter scans the full arch of sky. Curving panels of the dome frame his watch for action.

Thoughts crowd in on Coulter whenever action draws near. His chest fills with a familiar weakness as he waits. Not fear exactly, he judges, but a tight, helpless feeling. It grows and grows with the waiting before the strike. That tension gives the short tale its human center. Space hardware matters less here than nerves under strain. Readers get a compact story of a man braced for a launch he dreads.
22662-the-mummy-s-foot:
The Mummy's Foot is a short fantastic tale by Théophile Gautier. A writer in the story buys an ancient Egyptian foot to use as a paperweight. He dreams more than he bargained for. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Gautier loved art objects, and his story begins in a curiosity shop full of treasures.

The sample lingers in that shop: cascades of silver-bright Chinese silks, waves of tinsel lit by a slanting sunbeam, and portraits of every era smiling through yellowed varnish. In such a den, a mummy's foot is the least strange thing for sale. The tale that follows mixes humor with the fantastic. It is one of Gautier's most charming short works, light as the foot itself.
22865-critical-miscellanies-vol-2-of-3-e:
John Morley profiles the French statesman Turgot in this essay from the second volume of Critical Miscellanies. Turgot entered the world in Paris in May of 1727. His fifty-odd years covered the central decades of the seventeen hundreds. Morley calls that span the exact period of preparation for the Revolution.

The essay follows Turgot's reforms, his brief power, and his fall, asking why a capable minister failed inside a rotting system. Morley writes crisp, confident Victorian biography, with ideas always in the foreground. Readers meet both a man and a moment, the last real chance to repair old France from within. The piece suits anyone who likes history told through character under pressure.
22924-pathfinder-or-the-missing-tenderfo:
A sign on the trail halts the boys in Pathfinder, or The Missing Tenderfoot. Hold on, one calls. A stick stands upright in the path, and a piece of new birch bark sits fast in its split end, gripped like the jaws of a vise. Trail craft, in this world, is a language to be read.

The story belongs to the great age of American boys' outdoor series. A tenderfoot has gone missing, and woodcraft, tracking, and cool heads must find him. Every snapped twig and marked tree becomes evidence. The dialogue runs brisk and slangy, the woods thick and inviting. Readers who grew up on campfire fiction will know the pleasures here. New readers get a clean specimen of the breed.
22958-one-shot:
Eggs and clearance ratings open One Shot, a story of official investigation. Identifying the egg was the job, the narrator says, and the records show his outfit entering the affair officially at that point. Anderton had spent the previous hour keeping the wires to Washington steaming, winning authorization to spend money on the team. Their clearance stood at C and R, clean and routine.

That dry bureaucratic voice sells the strangeness that follows. Paperwork, approvals, and expense accounts frame an object no file can quite hold. The contrast is the engine of the piece, and a modern one. Readers who like their wonders processed through sensible men with forms will enjoy watching procedure meet the inexplicable here.
551-the-land-that-time-forgot:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens his Caspak trilogy with a manuscript found off Greenland in this lost-world tale. On 3 June 1916, a liner is torpedoed, and survivors reach Caprona, an island where life climbs from ape to man across its breadth. The narrator, stranded and doomed, writes his story in three months of terror.

Burroughs writes with pulp energy, mixing U-boats, dinosaurs, and tribal wars. Caprona's secret, that time itself seems to evolve life, grips the tale. The book charms as a bold adventure, where modern men meet a world long dead to science.
552-the-people-that-time-forgot:
Edgar Rice Burroughs continues the Caspak saga in this sequel to The Land That Time Forgot. Bowen Tyler's manuscript, carried to his father at Santa Monica, tells of a lost world where life climbs an evolutionary ladder island-wide. A torpedoed liner, a yacht, and a search party frame the tale.

Burroughs writes brisk pulp adventure, with ape men, dinosaurs, and tribes at war. The people that time forgot live by tooth and spear, yet dream of higher life. The book charms as a lost-world romance, where a modern man must fight his way through ages in a single island.
738-the-puzzle-of-dickens-s-last-plot:
Andrew Lang took up the riddle of Edwin Drood, the novel Charles Dickens left unfinished at his death. Lang notes that Dickens, from Bleak House onward, worked hard at plot, and he asks what end the master had planned for his last tale. The book, issued in 1905, weighs the clues Dickens left in the text and in his talk with friends.

Lang tests rival theories about the fate of Edwin, the role of John Jasper, and the mystery at the heart of the story. He argues with care, citing scenes and letters, and he admits where proof runs out. The volume remains a classic piece of literary detection, for readers who love both Dickens and the game of solving an author's last puzzle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbot:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abbot treats the head of a community of at least twelve monks. Its name comes from abba, Syriac for the Hebrew ab, meaning father. It was first used in Syria and Egypt as a title of honour for any monk of venerable age or eminent holiness. At first it implied no authority over a community.

From the East the word passed westward and came to designate an abbey's superior. The article treats its historical origin, the office's nature, kinds of abbots, election, benediction, authority, rights and privileges, assistance at councils, and distribution of abbots. Monastic communities were first organised in Egypt early in the fourth century, when St. Anthony directed the hermits gathered about him in the Thebaid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-john-a:
Alexis John Augustine Bachelot was Prefect Apostolic of the Sandwich Islands, born in France in February 1796 and dead at sea in December 1837. He entered the Picpus preparatory seminary at Paris aged ten and took vows in the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts at Cahors in February 1813. After theology at the Irish College in Paris, he was ordained a priest in 1820 and became its rector. Four years later he became superior of the preparatory seminary at Tours.

Sent to the Sandwich Islands, he reached Honolulu in July 1827 with Father Armand and three lay brothers. Refused residence, the priests landed anyway and Bachelot said the first Mass in the Hawaiian Islands the next morning. The Protestant mission persuaded the chiefs to expel them, and in December 1831 Bachelot and Father Short were forcibly shipped to California. A fresh attempt in 1837 landed unmolested at Honolulu, and Bachelot wrote a Hawaiian grammar, dictionary, and catechisms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-robert-j:
Turgot, Baron de L'Aulne, minister, born 1727, died 1781. Destined for the Church in his youth, he wrote on God's existence and love. In 1750, as Sorbonne prior, he marked his transition with discourses on religion and the mind, mingling true and false ideas. There he foretold the colonies' separation from England.

Philosophy prevailed, and he declined Holy orders. In 1752 he entered the magistracy, and in 1761 became Limoges intendant. After a short marine ministry term, Louis XVI made him controller-general in 1774. This caused discontent over corn prices, but Turgot thought he could quell it. His territorial tax edict displeased the privileged, and his guild suppression destroyed medieval organization. By depriving the Hôtel Dieu of its Friday meat privilege, dispensing Sunday Mass time, and changing the coronation oath, he angered clergy. He was disgraced in 1776. In retirement he wrote for Price and Franklin on taxation. Dussard and Daire edited his works in 1844.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-vero:
Augustin Verot was the third Bishop of Savannah and the first Bishop of St Augustine, born at Le Puy in France in 1804, who died at St Augustine in 1876. He studied at St Sulpice in Paris, was ordained in 1828, joined the Sulpicians, and came to Baltimore in 1830. He taught science, philosophy, and theology at St Mary's until 1853, then spent four years in mission work. Named Vicar Apostolic of Florida in 1857, he found a vicariate with only three priests.

With help sought in France, he repaired churches at St Augustine, Jacksonville, and Key West. He built new ones at Tampa, Fernandina, Palatka, Mandarin, and Tallahassee. Moved to Savannah in 1861 while keeping Florida, he led his people through Civil War ruin and Reconstruction with unfailing courage. He visited his whole diocese yearly, founded churches and schools, revived the memory of Florida's early martyrs, and wrote a noted Pastoral on Slavery and a Catechism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commendatory-:
Michael Ott's entry defines a commendatory abbot as an ecclesiastic or layman holding an abbey in commendam. He draws its revenues, and if a cleric, may hold some jurisdiction. He does not rule its inner monastic discipline. At first only vacant abbeys, or houses briefly lacking a superior, went in commendam, until a superior was chosen. A house held in commendam stays provisional, unlike one held in titulum, a permanent benefice.

As early as Gregory the Great, from 590 to 604, vacant abbeys went in commendam to bishops driven from their sees by invaders. Abuse grew grave in the eighth century, when kings claimed the right to set commendatory abbots over monasteries. Popes and councils then tried to regulate the practice. Ott sets out the holder's powers: over temporal affairs, over a separate abbot's income where one exists, and, for vacant houses, nearly all rights of an abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-auguste:
This biographical entry presents Count Auguste-Arthur Beugnot, a French historian and statesman born in 1797 and dead in 1865, son of a minister under several regimes. It follows his early prize-winning essays, his election to the Academy of Inscriptions, and his editions of medieval legal texts that scholars still value.

Beugnot's histories of the Jews of the West and of the fall of paganism brought him fame, though the latter was placed on the Index and later eclipsed by Seeck. His editions of the Assizes of Jerusalem, the Customs of Beauvaisis, and the Olim registers of the Paris Parlement remain important for feudal and customary law. Entering politics in 1841, he later defended the Church and liberty of teaching in the great education debates of 1849 and 1850.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didot:
Didot is the name of a Paris family of printers and publishers. Their presses shaped French bookmaking from the early eighteenth century onward. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with Francois Didot, who opened a bookshop in 1713. He won a royal printing charter in 1754 and led the booksellers of Paris as their syndic.

His son Francois-Ambroise carried the firm further with fine sets of French classics for the court. Later Didots issued a great Greek thesaurus in nine volumes. The entry traces a family trade across four generations, from a single shop on the Quai des Grands-Augustins to editions prized by lovers of fine books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-genico:
Edward Genicot was a Belgian Jesuit teacher of moral theology, born at Antwerp in 1856 and dead at Louvain in 1900. After a brilliant course at the Jesuit college in his home city he entered the Society in 1872. He taught humanities and rhetoric at Ghent and Antwerp, and after ordination and a public defence in all theology he taught canon law, then moral theology, at Louvain from 1889.

Pupils liked him for the solid, clear way he taught. His Theologiae Moralis Institutiones, first issued in 1896, drew on Ballerini-Palmieri and won praise for plain statement, firm judgment, and honest daring in following a principle to its end. A second work, Casus Conscientiae, drawn largely from real cases, came out after his death and gave confessors true-to-life examples rather than bare theory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-rena:
Eusebius Renaudot was a French scholar of the age of Louis XIV, an apologist for the Catholic Church and one of the great Orientalists of his time. He was born at Paris in 1648 and educated by the Jesuits. He joined the Oratorians in 1666 but left them soon after for reasons of health, and he never took more than minor orders. His talent and love of study won him the friendship of Bossuet, whom he backed against Richard Simon, Fénelon, and the Jesuits.

Most of his books were written to defend the Church as well as to advance learning. They include the later volumes of the Perpétuité de la foi against the Calvinists, a defense of that work, and editions of homilies of Gennadius on the Eucharist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilbert-folio:
Gilbert Foliot was Bishop of London, born early in the twelfth century of an Anglo-Norman family, who died at London in 1186. A Cluny monk who rose to prior, he served as abbot at Abbeville and Gloucester before becoming Bishop of Hereford in 1147. In 1163 he was moved to London, a rare translation backed by Becket and Pope Alexander III. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a learned, eloquent, and austere administrator.

He had backed Empress Matilda and advised Archbishop Theobald, yet in the great quarrel between Henry II and St. Thomas Becket he stood firmly with the king. At Clarendon and Northampton, and through the long exile negotiations, his name led the bishops against his archbishop. His protests against a renewed excommunication in 1170 helped bring about, indirectly, Becket's martyrdom. He may have opposed Becket's manner more than his aims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-abbot:
Henry Abbot, a layman and convert living at Holden in Yorkshire, was martyred at York on 4 July 1597. According to Challoner's account, a Protestant minister imprisoned in York Castle feigned repentance and a wish to embrace Catholicism in order to regain favour. The Catholic prisoners directed him to Abbot to find a priest who could receive him. Abbot brought the man to Esquire Stapleton's house at Carlton, but no priest was found.

The minister then betrayed the group to the magistrates. Abbot and his companions confessed that they had explained the Catholic faith to him, and all were found guilty and sentenced to die. Errington, Knight, and Gibson died on the scaffold on 29 November 1596, while Abbot was reprieved until the following July. He was pronounced Venerable in 1886, a recognition of a death that followed directly from an act of hospitality and religious instruction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-amyot:
Jacques Amyot was bishop of Auxerre, grand almoner of France, and a man of letters. He was born on 30 October 1513 and died on 6 February 1593. He studied at Paris' Collège de France. There he earned his keep by doing menial work for fellow students. Naturally slow, he amassed wide classical learning through uncommon diligence. He took his Master of Arts degree at nineteen.

A secretary of state hired him as tutor to his children. He recommended Amyot to Marguerite d'Angoulême, sister of Francis I. Amyot became professor of Greek and Latin at Bourges university. During ten years there he translated the Greek novel Theagenes and Chariclea. He also translated several of Plutarch's Lives. Francis I rewarded those works with the abbey of Bellozane. The entry follows a poor student turned court scholar and translator.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-callo:
French etcher, engraver, and painter Jacques Callot was born at Nancy in 1592. He died there on 28 March 1635. His father Jean Callot was a Lorraine noble and herald-at-arms. He wanted his son to become a soldier or a priest. But the boy's artistic bent proved intense and precocious. Even schoolboy work showed a grasp of character. The bizarre and humorous, especially among lower folk, drew him most.

Before twelve he had studied design with help from Henriet Israel and Dumange Crocq. In 1604 he ran away to Italy with a band of gypsies, hoping to reach Rome. He stopped at Florence and studied engraving under Remigio Gallina. He copied works of the masters there. The entry follows a runaway boy toward mastery of the etched line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-talbot:
James Talbot's father was George Talbot, and his brother was the fourteenth Earl of Shrewsbury; James himself was the fourth son. Born in 1726, he died in 1790. He is best known as the last priest indicted in public courts for saying Mass. Schooled at Douai, a college he enriched generously, he was consecrated coadjutor bishop to Dr Challoner in 1759, at thirty-three.

Twice as bishop, in 1769 and 1771, he was tried on information from the informer Payne and cleared each time for lack of evidence. Judge Lord Mansfield clearly favored him, though Mansfield was no friend to Catholics as such. His house was wrecked in the Gordon Riots in 1780. On Challoner's death in 1781 he became vicar apostolic of the London district, ruling it nine years, retired at Hammersmith and famed for unbounded charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-tissot:
French draughtsman and painter James Tissot, born Joseph-Jacques Tissot, was born at Nantes on 15 October 1836. He died at Buillon, Doubs, on 3 August 1902. He studied at Paris' Academy of Fine Arts and in the studios of Ingres and Flandrin. During that period he learned the darker side of Parisian moral and political life. His first salon paintings drew great attention, especially one showing Faust meeting Gretchen, now in the Luxembourg Museum.

When the Commune took power, Tissot fled to England. He feared conflict with the government over his brother's political intrigues. In England he won fame as a portrait and genre painter. Yet Tissot was more illustrator than painter, as his brilliant watercolor series La femme à Paris shows. In careful, correct work done with much dash, he pictured Parisian women of every class. The entry follows an illustrator of modern Paris life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-bagot:
Jean Bagot, a French Jesuit theologian born at Rennes in 1591 and dead in Paris in 1664. He taught letters, philosophy, and theology for decades and served as theologian to his order's general. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1611 and spent thirteen years teaching theology alone.

Bagot's chief work, the Apologeticus Fidei, defended the faith in parts issued from 1645 onward, including a treatise on penance. He attacked new teaching on grace and defended the rights of bishops and the freedom of the faithful in confession against rival clergy. Paris theologians censured some of his claims, but after his defence the censure was lifted, closing a long and public dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Biot, a French physicist and mathematician born in Paris in 1774 and dead there in 1862, moved from soldiering to science and held chairs across a long life. After the École Polytechnique he taught at Beauvais, then at twenty-six took the chair of mathematical physics at the Collège de France.

Biot rose with Gay-Lussac in a balloon in 1804 to thirteen thousand feet, testing air at height. He joined the great survey that fixed the metre by measuring a meridian arc. He belonged in turn to three classes of the Institute, for science, inscriptions, and letters. His work joined exact measure, astronomy, and optics in a single exacting career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François-Anne Landriot, a French bishop born near Autun in 1816 and dead at Reims in 1874. He was ordained in 1839 and rose from seminary superior in 1842 to vicar-general, bishop of La Rochelle in 1856, and archbishop of Reims in 1867.

At La Rochelle Landriot restored the cathedral, organised mission and Peter's Pence collections, and won fame as a preacher who announced God's word himself. At Reims he preached Advent and Lent courses, raised funds for the papal army, founded schools and an asylum for the aged, and softened German rigour during the 1870 occupation. At Vatican Council he thought infallibility ill-timed, yet urged full acceptance once defined.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-jacques-:
Jean-Jacques Casot, the last surviving Jesuit of old Canada, was born at Liège in 1728 and died at Quebec in 1800. With him ended the line of Ignatius's sons who laboured in Canada through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and at his death the Society stood extinct in New France.

Casot joined as a lay brother in Paris in 1753, sailed for Canada late in 1756, and worked as cook at Quebec college. Bishop Briand ordained him priest precisely to keep the Society alive as long as possible. Humble and devout, he spent his inherited property on works of zeal and charity, and on his death Jesuit property in Canada passed to the British Crown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-and-seba:
John Cabot was the Genoese-born navigator who reached the American mainland for England in 1497, before Columbus. After fifteen years at Venice earned him citizenship in 1476, he settled in England about 1490 with his three sons. By letters patent of March 1496, Henry VII licensed him and his sons to seek heathen lands to the west, east, and north under the English flag.

Sailing from Bristol in May 1497 in the Matthew with eighteen men, Cabot made land on 24 June. By his son Sebastian's chart the land was near Cape Breton Island, though some scholars place the landing in Labrador. A second expedition of five ships and three hundred men sailed in 1498, pushing north to drifting ice before coasting past Newfoundland. The entry weighs the charts and claims behind England's title to North America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-talbot:
John Talbot was an English Catholic layman whose life was a long round of recusant imprisonment and bail. Born about 1535, only son and heir of Sir John Talbot of Grafton, he entered Lincoln's Inn in 1556. He fathered George Talbot, priest and ninth Earl of Shrewsbury. Passing through Smithfield in July 1580, he was present when the martyr Robert Johnson was recognized by the informer Sledd.

Committed to the Dean of Westminster that August, then to his brother-in-law's house in Aldersgate, he spent the next two decades moving between confinement and bail. His stops included Wisbech Castle in 1588 for hearing Mass, Broughton in 1590, Ely gaol in 1593, and Banbury Castle in 1596. He paid fines of 120 pounds for recusancy and took leaves to take the waters at Bath for his health. His case shows, in miniature, the grinding machinery of Elizabethan persecution of Catholic gentlemen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-jacoto:
Joseph Jacotot was a French educator who claimed that anyone can teach himself anything. Born at Dijon in 1770, he taught classical literature at nineteen and later held chairs in sciences, languages, mathematics, and law. His support for the Empire forced him into exile at the Restoration, and in 1818 he became professor of French at Louvain.

At Louvain he knew no Flemish or Dutch, while his pupils knew no French. Giving them Fénelon's Télémaque in both tongues, he had them memorize and compare a little more each day. To his surprise they mastered spelling and grammar alone. From this grew his Universal Teaching, built on the student's own effort and the links between all knowledge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-maria-:
Joseph Maria Amiot was a French Jesuit missionary who opened China to European readers. Born at Toulon in 1718, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1737 and reached China in 1740. He won the trust of Emperor Qianlong, whose Tatar tongue he spoke fluently, and mastered Chinese, physics, history, mathematics, and music.

Amiot poured his knowledge into a vast correspondence and into the Mémoires on Chinese history, science, arts, and customs, published at Paris from 1776 to 1789. He wrote a Tatar-Manchu grammar and dictionary, a table of Chinese emperors, and studies of Chinese music, weights, and warfare. He died at Peking in 1793.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judas-iscario:
Judas Iscariot was the apostle who betrayed Jesus to his enemies. His name joins Judas, the Greek form of Judah, meaning praised, with Iscariot, a man of Kerioth, a town in Judah. That origin marked him out among apostles who were otherwise Galilean, and some suggest it bred a lack of sympathy with them.

Scripture tells little of Judas beyond his call, his treachery, and his death, and never names him without the betrayal. John adds that his father was Simon and that Judas kept the purse. He protested Mary's ointment not from care for the poor but because, as a thief, he took what was put in.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lay-abbot: A 1913 entry on the Lay Abbot — the secular holder. Johann Peter Kirsch unfolds its medieval lore. He seized the abbey's revenues. The monks mourned the worldly yoke. The ages knew its abuses. Its 1907 study is famed. Its medieval form is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lot: This 1913 reference piece on Lot — the rescued nephew. Francis X.E. Albert unfolds the Genesis tale. He fled the doomed cities. The angels led the trembling sire. The Book keeps his story. His Zoar flight is famed. His wife's pillar is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-veuillo: A 1913 entry on Veuillot — the Ultramontane journalist. Eugène Tavernier honors his famous Univers. His pen thundered for the papal cause. France knew the fiery name. The nineteenth century told his tale. His 1883 death is famed. His 1833 Univers is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marc-lescarbo: This 1913 reference piece on Lescarbot — the Acadian historian. Lionel Lindsay honors his famous Histoire. His pen chronicled the New World. The scholars prized the early tome. The seventeenth century knew his name. His 1629 death is famed. His 1609 Histoire is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oates-s-plot: Titus Oates invented the Popish Plot of 1678, a fantasy of Catholic conspiracy that sent innocent priests and peers to the scaffold. This entry exposes his lies, his victims, and his disgrace. The lie that killed: his perjury sent twenty-two innocent men to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pauline-marie: Pauline Jaricot founded the Society for the Propagation of the Faith in 1822 with her pennies for the missions. This entry traces her foundation, her charity, and her beatification. The girl who funded the missions: her pennies built the Church's mission fund.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-talbot: Peter Talbot was the archbishop of Dublin who suffered in the Popish Plot's aftermath. This entry traces his career, his imprisonment, and his death. The martyr-archbishop of the plot years: his lonely prison death in Dublin crowned his long faithful witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-helyot: Pierre Hélyot was the Franciscan whose history of the religious orders filled eight volumes. This entry covers his career, his great work, and its value. The historian of the monastic orders: his eight fat volumes catalogued every monastic habit in Christendom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-joseph: Pierre-Joseph Chaumonot was the Jesuit who founded the Huron mission of Lorette. This entry traces his mission, his chapel, and his autobiography. The founder of the Lorette Hurons: his little chapel mirrored Loreto's Holy House exactly in miniature form and spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-lescot: Pierre Lescot was the architect of the Louvre's Renaissance wing. This entry covers his career, his palace, and his art. The builder of the French Renaissance court: his noble Louvre wing endures today in sculptured stone for all to admire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-martia: Pierre-Martial Cibot was the Jesuit whose Chinese memoirs enlightened Europe. This entry covers his mission, his writings, and their influence. The sinologist of the Peking mission: his learned memoirs taught curious Europe all about distant imperial China and its rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-aubert-s: Vertot was the historian of the Knights of Malta. This entry notes his histories, his style, and his fame. The chronicler of the revolutions: his proud Malta filled the volumes with glory and fame and honor and praise and wonder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-andrew-: St. Andrew the Scot was the abbot of the Irish monks in Germany. This entry notes his abbey, his life, and his fame. The Schottenkloster's holy abbot: his Irish monks served the Germans in Bavaria's towns in the 1000s' decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-gunpowder: The Gunpowder Plot was the treason of 1605. This long entry examines its Catesby, its Fawkes, and its failure. The conspiracy of the Fifth of November: their dark powder crowned the cellar in the 1605 of the James in the palace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophraste-r: Renaudot was the father of the French press. This long entry examines his 1631, his Gazette, and his fame. The physician of the Paris poor: his famed Gazette crowned Paris in the 1631 of the Richelieu in the old court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-talbot: Talbot was the priest of the mission. This entry traces his 1600s, his England, and his labors. The cleric of the penal times: his hidden labors crowned England in the 1620s of the mission in the truly very old north.
doe-osti-3004691-estimation-methodology-: Fusion plant impacts got estimated, and this DOE methodology covers hypothetical downwind effects. The pages detail the findings. The safety folks get their tool. The impacts were downwind hypothetical. The tool was safety. The plants were fusion. The impacts were hypothetical.
doe-osti-3017684-characterization-of-per: Brain-computer light links getting mapped got their DOE closeout, and this final charts the interfaces. The pages detail the report results. The computing folks get their closeout. The links were photonic. The results were report. The interfaces were charts.
doe-osti-3018256-cost-analysis-of-heavy-: Heavy-duty PEM got cost-analyzed, and this DOE text prices stationary power plants. The pages detail the vehicle findings. The energy folks get their data. The plants were stationary power. The data were energy. The membrane was proton. The duty was heavy.
doe-osti-3364279-enhanced-component-perf: Motor pumps got performance-studied, and this DOE text covers 1998-2024. The pages detail the enhanced findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The study was component. The data were nuclear. The 1998-2024 were pumps. The driven were motor. The pumps were study.
doe-osti-3378276-cyber-labeling-for-ener: IIoT got cyber-labeled, and this DOE text covers energy industrial labels. The pages detail the labeling findings. The security folks get their data. The labeling was cyber. The data were security. The IoT were industrial. The energy were labels.
doe-osti-3380404-high-capacity-hydrogen-: H2 getters got high-capacity-gotten, and this DOE text covers isotope getters. The pages detail the capacity findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The getters were hydrogen. The data were nuclear. The isotope were getters. The nuclear were folks.
doe-osti-3385010-evaluation-of-the-dose-: Hot vaults got dose-evaluated, and this DOE text covers beam-on operations. The pages detail the process findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The station was second target. The data were nuclear. The target were second. The beam-on were operation.
govdocs-archive_org-PointsOfDifferenceBe:
Rev. F. Laun wrote his short catechetical pamphlet in 1915 to teach Catholics where their church parts ways with Protestant teaching. It carries the imprimatur of Cardinal John Farley, Archbishop of New York, marking it as approved church instruction for its day.

Laun works through the disputed points one by one, setting the Catholic position beside the Protestant one on matters of doctrine and practice. The tone is plain and direct, aimed at classroom use and at readers weighing conversion. It survives as a clear snapshot of how American Catholics explained their faith to others a century ago.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GarrisonJimQuot:
The Los Angeles Free Press devoted its November 10-17, 1967 issue to a speech by Jim Garrison. The underground paper printed the full text of the district attorney's Los Angeles address. In it Garrison criticized President Lyndon B. Johnson over the Kennedy assassination, under a headline saying Johnson protects assassins.

A prosecutor accusing a sitting president in print was extraordinary, and the underground press carried it gladly. The Free Press gave Garrison's words entire pages while mainstream outlets handled him with care. The issue preserves the speech whole, in the paper that was proud to print it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KissingerPlot_K:
Francine du Plessix Gray's 'The Politics of Salvation: II' examines the Harrisburg conspiracy case of the early 1970s. Prosecutors alleged a plot to kidnap Henry Kissinger, then the national security adviser. The piece is the second part of her study of the case and of the people pulled into it.

Among the figures Gray writes about are Boyd Douglas and Mary Chenoweth. The case grew out of the antiwar movement and the government's reliance on an informer inside it. Her account asks how far the evidence really went. It also asks what the prosecution revealed about the era's fear of dissent, and about the thin line between watching a movement and building a case against it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KorffKalTotalAn: Transcript number 972 of Larry King Live, broadcast by CNN on November 22, 1993, marked thirty years since the assassination of President Kennedy. The program's title for the episode was 'The Kennedy Assassination: Thirty Years Later.' Show transcripts preserve the questions and answers word for word. This one records how the case was being argued on television three decades after Dallas, in a format built around a host, his guests, and the callers who reached the studio.
lineage-life-and-labors-of-jose-rizal-ph:
Austin Craig studies José Rizal's lineage, life, and labors here. Manila published the biography in 1913. Craig taught Oriental history at the University of the Philippines. James Alexander Robertson supplied the introduction.

Craig calls the book a study of free ideas' growth. He dedicates it to Philippine youth, Rizal's fair hope of the fatherland. Rizal wrote, he notes, for a coming instructed generation. Public school education, Craig argues, now gives youth Rizal's democratic viewpoint. Fifty-five Blair-Robertson volumes supplied Craig's documentary background on the Philippines. Robertson's introduction frames Rizal for American territory readers in 1913.
nasa-tm-19690095502-earth-resources-surv:
H. T. Betz, of IIT Research Institute in Chicago, wrote this January 1968 technical letter, Interagency Report NASA-101. It belongs to the Earth Resources Survey Program and was released in open files by the U.S. Geological Survey. His subject is the remote measurement of rhodamine B concentration in water. The dye glows under light, which makes it a tracer hydrologists can follow.

Injected fluorescent dyes let researchers track how dissolved material spreads through rivers and streams. Measuring the glow from a distance would map that spread without sampling every point by hand. Betz's letter takes up the measurement problem itself for this one dye. The work was performed under a NASA contract tied to the survey program.
notes-on-nursing-what-it-is-and-what-it-:
Florence Nightingale wrote Notes on Nursing to say what nursing is, and what it is not. This New York copy came from D. Appleton and Company in 1898. Her preface denies that the notes form a rule or a manual for teaching nurses. They give hints for thought, she says, to women in charge of others' health.

Every woman, she argues, has charge of somebody's health at some time, child or invalid. In other words, every woman is a nurse. Sanitary knowledge, how to keep a body free of disease, differs from medical knowledge. Only a profession can hold the second, she says. Contents begin with ventilation and warming, and the health of houses.
old-put-the-patriot:
Frederick Albion Ober wrote this life of Israel Putnam. Appleton published it in New York in 1904. Putnam was a soldier known as Old Put. The contents start with his birthplace and youth. Early chapters call him Old Wolf Putnam, the partisan fighter.

Later chapters treat frontier war, strategy, and woodcraft. Putnam becomes a prisoner and faces grave peril. He also campaigns in Cuba during the old wars. At home he keeps a tavern and gives advice. Ober writes a lively, patriotic life for general readers. The book honors a bold Revolutionary War hero.
rambles-beyond-railways-or-notes-in-corn:
Rambles Beyond Railways, or Notes in Cornwall Taken A-foot, by Wilkie Collins, is a walking tour of Cornwall. It is shown here in the new London edition of Richard Bentley, 1861. The book is dedicated to Henry C. Brandling, the companion of Collins's walk. The book was first written after a visit in the summer and autumn of 1850.

In his preface Collins admits that his title was strictly true only when he walked. Little more than a year later a second edition was called for. The all-conquering railway had meanwhile invaded Cornwall. It had contradicted him on his own title page.
the-abbot:
Sir Walter Scott wrote The Abbot as the sequel to The Monastery, with a front plate that shows Roland Graeme and Catherine Seton before Queen Mary. A new opening essay dated 1831 has Scott look back at the first book's cool welcome.

Scott grants that The Monastery felt much like a failure to him, though sellers did not grumble at its sales. He says fame is not won or lost by one book, yet a writer who does not move forward slips back. He wrote the sequel to test if the fault lay in the tale or the topic. Readers then get Mary, Queen of Scots, at Lochleven, her escape, and a page's divided loyalties.
the-adventure-of-the-devil-s-foot:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Adventure of the Devil's Foot as a Sherlock Holmes tale, told by Dr. Watson. Watson begins by noting how much Holmes hates fame, and how few of his notes have reached print in late years for that cause.

Holmes, he says, loved to hand the credit for a solved case to some staff officer and smile at the praise that missed its mark. Then a telegram from Holmes stuns Watson, since Holmes wires when a wire will serve and wrote: why not tell them of the Cornish horror, the strangest case he has handled. Readers get a tale of a weird poison and deaths in Cornwall that test Holmes's health and nerve.
the-blind-spot:
Austin Hall and Homer Eon Flint wrote a fantasy novel introduced here by Forrest J. Ackerman. Ackerman records that its first instalment appeared in Argosy All-Story Weekly for May 14, 1921. A cover by Modest Stein showed a girl of another dimension, called the Nervina.

Behind her stood a huge flaming ball, an ancient quay, and a city of spires, domes, and minarets above blue waters. Ackerman traces reprints in Famous Fantastic Mysteries and Fantastic Novels, now collectors' items. Flint and Hall were already popular with readers of imaginative fiction. Who wrote which part, Ackerman notes, has long been a question among fans.
the-bontoc-igorot:
Albert Ernest Jenks wrote The Bontoc Igorot for the Ethnological Survey in Manila. His note of February 3, 1904 sends the study to Dean C. Worcester, Secretary of the Interior. He asks that it stand as Volume I of a set of science studies on the Philippine Islands. The work came out of a two-month trip in late 1902 and a five-month stay in Bontoc from January 1903.

Jenks chose the Igorot of Bontoc, in north Luzon, as a clear type of the old hill folk who farmed the high land. He lived there with his wife and also spent six weeks among the Benguet Igorot. Most plates are from photos, some by Worcester in April 1903 and some by Charles Martin, the state photographer, in January 1903. The aim was to show the life and ways of the Luzon hill folk from close study on the ground.
the-idiot: John Kendrick Bangs wrote this humorous book. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in 1895. Bangs dedicated it to William K. Otis. Only the title pages and illustrations list are present here. The comic narrative itself does not appear. The captions sketch a world of trains and talk. A man asks for another cup. Another scene gives the nuisance of having to pay. A woman could not possibly get aboard again. Tickets for two are demanded. A fisherman fishes all day without luck.
the-land-that-time-forgot:
Edgar Rice Burroughs frames his lost world tale as a found manuscript dated from June 3, 1916. A narrator fishing near Cape Farewell in Greenland finds the account and reads of three brief months packed with sights no other living eye had seen. The writer claims a dead world survives in a hidden pocket of the earth.

Burroughs mixes sea travel, war era dates, and deep time in the opening pages. The manuscript voice insists that fate has sealed his doom in that place. Readers enter a pulp adventure built on a journal that should never have reached home.
the-landloper-the-romance-of-a-man-on-fo:
Holman Day published his novel in 1915, subtitled the romance of a man on foot. Walker Farr walks a dusty country road on a bright June morning, bareheaded under arching elms. He looks young, strong, and sunburnt, yet his worn clothes mark him as a vagrant to others.

A passing car leaves a brief memory of a girl profile, and a farmer offers him work with open suspicion. Day sets up a puzzle in the opening scene. Farr carries the face and manner of somebody important while choosing the life of the road.
the-last-shot:
Frederick Palmer published his war novel in 1914 and addressed readers directly about its roots. He had watched many wars as an observer under fire, sharing marches and camp fellowship without bearing arms. That odd career, he says, began by chance and spread across the earth.

Palmer claims every war showed him the same human pattern. Sides trade places in his sympathy, since courage, sacrifice, and grief look alike in both lines. His story follows that pattern of rising passion, conflict, defeat or victory, and peace enjoyed too late by tired nations everywhere.
the-man-with-the-clubfoot: Valentine Williams's The Man with the Clubfoot is dated 1918. Only a publisher's summary headed "What This Story Is About" and part of the contents are present, so the novel does not appear. The summary calls Clubfoot a most ingenious and sinister secret agent in Europe, assigned to regain an indiscreet letter written by the Kaiser. An officer, Desmond Okewood, sets out to thwart him and to find his brother, penetrating Germany in disguise. Chapter titles include I Seek a Bed in Rotterdam and The Cipher with the Invoice.
the-memoirs-of-general-baron-de-marbot: Only the Project Gutenberg header is present for The Memoirs of General the Baron de Marbot, so none of the memoir itself appears here. The header names the translator as Oliver C. Colt and dates the release to November 2000, as etext 2401. A note adds that the zip version also carries four bitmap images: maps or plans connected with Austerlitz, Friedland, and Leipzig. The remaining lines are standard Gutenberg cautions about copyright, donations, and corrected editions.
the-people-that-time-forgot:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The People That Time Forgot. Chapter One opens with a narrator who has carried Bowen Tyler's manuscript to the Tyler library at Santa Monica. He admits he still doubts its truth. Bowen was once a notorious practical joker at college. The narrator half wishes he had sent the manuscript by express instead of bringing it himself.

Mr. Tyler, senior, is expected hourly, his yacht Toreador overdue from Honolulu. The narrator reviews the known facts. Bowen sailed for France to join the American Ambulance, and his liner was torpedoed. Neither he nor Miss La Rue was listed among survivors. Rescue by an English tug and the capture of a German submarine seemed possible. The lost-world tale begins as a found manuscript.
the-puzzle-of-dickens-s-last-plot:
Andrew Lang examines the unfinished mystery Dickens left behind, in an edition issued at London in 1905 by Chapman and Hall. His introduction, drawing on Forster, argues that from Bleak House onward Dickens worked hard at construction and at plots full of secrets.

Lang weighs that care against the freer energy of Pickwick and Nicholas Nickleby, and links Dickens to Wilkie Collins and to the detective novel. The question is what the final plot of the last novel was meant to be. Readers of Dickens gain a critic's reconstruction that treats curiosity and surprise as serious parts of the novelist's art.
the-simpkins-plot:
G. A. Birmingham's The Simpkins Plot was published by T. Nelson and Sons in London and Edinburgh. Birmingham dedicated it to R. H., recalling summer evenings drifting home. They were untroubled then by the love affairs of Simpkins, he jokes. Chapter one opens at Euston station. The platform is crowded, and porters' barrows are piled high with luggage.

In the last week of July, the Irish mail runs heavy with passengers, Birmingham writes. Schoolboys escape home for the summer holidays with portmanteaux and play-boxes. Sportsmen and keen lawyers head for Donegal or Clare for fishing. Tourists hold tickets promising rounds of famous beauty spots. Members of the House of Lords travel back to stately Irish mansions with their wives. Great people in drawing-rooms, such travellers lose their grandeur on the platform, he observes.
